modelResponse.episodeSummary: Walter J. Osei, 70M, critical episode, symptomatic bradycardia
keyECGEvidence: morphology AV dissociation; wide QRS escape; tall peaked symmetric T waves; flattened P waves
preEventNote Progressive PR prolongation then AV dissociation; QRS widening over 20 min
modelResponse.mechanism: Hyperkalemia causes progressive AV nodal block and conduction disturbances, leading to complete heart block. It also causes characteristic ECG changes like peaked T waves and QRS widening.

rejectedAlternatives.why: The atrial rate is 84 bpm, which is not profoundly slow. The primary issue is AV dissociation, not sinus node failure. The ECG shows AV dissociation, not sinus arrest.

rejectedAlternatives.alternative: Medication Effect (e.g., Beta-blocker, Calcium Channel Blocker, Digoxin)
rejectedAlternatives.why: Patient is not on beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers. Digoxin toxicity can cause bradycardia and AV block, but the prominent hyperkalemia and associated ECG changes (peaked T waves, QRS widening) make hyperkalemia the more likely primary cause. Home meds do not include these agents.

While ischemia can cause AV block, the clinical context (missed dialysis, ESRD) and lab findings (severe hyperkalemia) strongly point towards hyperkalemia as the etiology. No specific evidence of ischemia is provided.

recommendedActions: Administer IV calcium gluconate (to stabilize cardiac membrane)
Administer IV insulin and glucose (to shift potassium intracellularly)
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate (to shift potassium intracellularly, address acidosis)
Initiate dialysis urgently (definitive treatment for hyperkalemia in ESRD)
Place temporary pacing lead (for symptomatic bradycardia/heart block)
Consider atropine (if pacing unavailable/delayed, but less likely effective for high-degree block)
Hold Lisinopril and Spironolactone (ACEi/ARB and potassium-sparing diuretics can worsen hyperkalemia)
